bear-suboptimality-constant.version: arXiv:1906.00949v2, 25 November 2019; NeurIPS 2019 main and supplement
bear-suboptimality-constant.summary: A Q-backup evaluates future rewards after the current action has already been chosen. Theorem 4.1 uses the difference between two such backups to bound the cost of restricting the policy. That difference can miss a reward lost by excluding the current action. Here both actions lead immediately to a zero-reward absorbing state, so the Q-backups agree. The constrained policy still loses the reward of one at the initial state.

checks.location: Theorem4.1 with Definitions4.1-4.2 and Assumption4.1; Appendix B.1
checks.claim: The performance guarantee bounds the constrained policy's state-value loss using approximation error and a suboptimality constant defined by the difference between two Q-backup operators at Q*.
checks.explanation: An action-value backup keeps the current action fixed and restricts only future choices. Its discrepancy can therefore miss an immediate reward excluded by the policy constraint. The proof switches to a state-value contraction argument while retaining the action-value discrepancy.
checks.demonstration: Use two states, an initial state $s_0$ and an absorbing state $s_1$, with $\gamma=1/2$. At $s_0$, actions $g$ and $b$ give rewards $1$ and $0$ and both move to $s_1$; all rewards at $s_1$ are zero. Let $\Pi$ contain only the policy choosing $b$, and use it as the behavior policy. Its discounted state marginal is $\mu(s_0)=\mu(s_1)=1/2$. For every $k\geq1$, $c(k)=2$ satisfies the concentrability condition, giving $C(\Pi)=2$. Initialize $Q_0=Q^*$, so $Q^*(s_0,g)=1$, $Q^*(s_0,b)=0$, and $Q^*(s_1,\cdot)=0$. Both backup operators preserve this function: $$\mathcal T^\Pi Q^*=\mathcal TQ^*=Q^*.$$ Thus $\delta=\alpha(\Pi)=0$ at every iteration. The only permitted policy nevertheless has $V^{\pi_k}(s_0)=0$, while $V^*(s_0)=1$. The theorem’s right side is zero and its left side is one.
checks.repair: Measure the loss of the current choice with $$\Delta_\Pi=\left\|V^*-\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\mathbb E_\pi Q^*\right\|_\infty.$$ For a rectangular policy restriction, which permits the allowed action distributions to be chosen independently at each state, define the state-value backup $T_\Pi V(s)=\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\mathbb E_\pi[r(s,a)+\gamma PV(s,a)]$. Here $r$ is the reward, $PV(s,a)$ is expected successor value, $T$ is the unrestricted state-value backup, and $V^\Pi$ is the fixed point of $T_\Pi$. Its contraction gives $$\|V^*-V^\Pi\|_\infty\leq\gamma\|V^*-V^\Pi\|_\infty+\|TV^*-T_\Pi V^*\|_\infty,$$ hence $\|V^*-V^\Pi\|_\infty\leq\Delta_\Pi/(1-\gamma)$. Here $\Delta_\Pi=1$, so the missing loss is detected. For approximate iteration, let $Q^\Pi$ be the fixed point of the constrained action-value backup. If a uniform residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$ satisfies $\|Q_{k+1}-\mathcal T^\Pi Q_k\|_\infty\leq\varepsilon$ and $\pi_k$ is constrained greedy for $Q_k$, contraction gives $\limsup_k\|Q_k-Q^\Pi\|_\infty\leq\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)$. Greedy selection then loses at most twice this action-value error per state, and policy evaluation adds a factor $1/(1-\gamma)$. Therefore $$\limsup_k\|V^{\pi_k}-V^*\|_\infty\leq\frac{\Delta_\Pi}{1-\gamma}+\frac{2\varepsilon}{(1-\gamma)^2}.$$ This uniform bound supplies a valid replacement without relying on the original distribution-weighted approximation coefficient.
checks.scope: The witness uses exact iteration, a singleton rectangular policy class, finite concentrability, and an ordinary finite discounted MDP. The repair fixes the constraint-cost term and supplies a uniform approximation-error guarantee. It does not preserve the original distribution-weighted approximation term.
checks.whyItMatters: A constraint can exclude the best first action even when it changes no continuation backup. Multiplying the original zero discrepancy by a larger constant cannot account for that loss; the discrepancy must include the current decision.

checks.claimContext: Theorem 4.1 bounds the value loss of the constrained greedy policies. The pointwise Bellman error is bounded by $\delta$, and $C(\Pi)$ is the stated concentrability coefficient. Here $\Pi$ is the allowed policy class, $Q^*$ is the optimal action-value function, $V^\pi$ is the state value of policy $\pi$, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. checks.location: Computational-universality reduction to a Neural GPU; Section4 reduction and AppendixB computational-power argument, full text, PDF pp.9 and13
checks.claim: Computational-universality reduction to a Neural GPU; Section4 reduction and AppendixB computational-power argument, full text, PDF pp.9 and13
checks.explanation: The specified substitutions do not identify the complete encoder update with a Neural GPU. Zero attention leaves normalization and coordinate additions, and the cited Neural GPU uses convolutional gates and a tanh update. The gap is repairable: a finite-symbol encoding can preserve both normalizations, both residual paths and all bounded coordinate additions. That construction establishes a uniform simulation with supplied tape and time budgets; a fixed finite tape or a step count fixed to the raw input length is not an unbounded computation.
checks.demonstration:
The displayed encoder applies
$$
\begin{aligned}
A&=\operatorname{LN}_1\!\left(H+P+\operatorname{Attn}(H+P)\right),\\
H'&=\operatorname{LN}_2\!\left(A+\operatorname{Transition}(A)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$
Zeroing the attention output gives $A=\operatorname{LN}_1(H+P)$. This is not the identity on arbitrary states: layer normalization satisfies
$$
\operatorname{LN}(x+a\mathbf1)=\operatorname{LN}(x).
$$
It discards the coordinate mean, which no fixed gain and bias can recover. With unit gain and zero bias, for example, $(2,0)$ becomes approximately $(1,-1)$. A carefully chosen finite code can avoid this obstruction.

The cited Neural GPU uses the gated update
$$
u(s)\odot s+[1-u(s)]\odot\tanh\!\left(U*(r(s)\odot s)+B\right),
$$
where $u,r$ are convolutional sigmoid gates. Merely selecting a convolution does not specify this map, cancel the transition residual, or absorb the normalization and coordinate additions. The source gives no invariant state code accomplishing those steps.

The resource convention is a separate requirement. A run for the original input length has a finite budget. To simulate arbitrary computations, one fixed parameter set must support supplied tape lengths and runtimes large enough for each finite computation. Turning that family into an unbounded computation also requires a resource-growth and halting-readout convention.
checks.repair:
Replace the exact-Neural-GPU identification with a direct local simulation. A Turing-machine tape has a finite cell alphabet $Q$ containing tape symbols and head/state markers; its legal configurations update by one fixed radius-one rule $f:Q^3\to Q$. Make $q=|Q|$ even, set $d=3q$, $L=100d$, and encode symbol $s$ by three copies of $L(e_s-q^{-1}\mathbf1)$. These codes have zero mean and variance $V=L^2(q-1)/q^2$. 

Set each normalization gain to $G=\sqrt{V+\epsilon}$ and its bias to zero, where $\epsilon$ is the normalization stabilizer. Each code is then fixed by normalization. Since each coordinate addition lies in $[-2,2]$, the first normalized output differs from its code by at most $E=4\sqrt d$ in Euclidean norm, uniformly in position and time. 

In the first separable convolution, route the three channel groups from offsets $-1,0,1$. For each symbol triple, sum its three selected coordinates to obtain $s_h$. Put $b_0=3L(1-1/q)-L/2$ and $w=L/2-3E>0$. The two ReLU channels $\operatorname{ReLU}((s_h-b_0)/w)-\operatorname{ReLU}((s_h-b_0)/w-1)$ give exactly one for the actual triple and zero for every other triple. Additional positive/negative ReLU channels carry each routed coordinate. The second separable convolution leaves triple channels in place and reverses the spatial routing of the identity channels. Its pointwise output is the selected next code minus $A_i$, cancelling the transition residual exactly. The second normalization fixes the next code. This uses $2q^3+2d$ hidden channels and fits the released width-three and width-five separable kernels. 

For a finite tape, place at least $2R+2$ genuine blank cells on each side of an input of length $\ell$, so $m\ge\ell+4R+4$. Each interior output depends only on the radius-one input triple: the reverse routing cancels the central residual even for states outside the codebook. Boundary errors can therefore travel at most one cell per step. Every cell within distance $R$ of the original input is still beyond their reach after $R$ steps, so this region contains the correct head, written tape and halting state. With dropout disabled and exact real arithmetic, induction proves the represented $R$-step computation. The same finite weights work for every budget.

This proves uniform finite-budget simulation. To compute until the simulated machine halts, add an explicit external allocator: retry budgets $R=1,2,4,\ldots$, initialize the corresponding guards, and read the halting state only within the protected region. The allocator grows memory and time; the encoder performs the machine transitions. This additional convention does not prove the unchanged claim with recurrence fixed to the original unpadded input length, nor a guarantee for learned adaptive halting.
checks.scope: This concerns the exact reduction in Section 4 of arXiv v3. The direct construction retains both normalizations, both residual paths and the bounded position/time additions, and proves an $R$-step simulation when $m\ge\ell+4R+4$ genuine tape cells are supplied. An external allocator is required for the unbounded-computation interpretation. The construction does not establish the original unpadded $T=m$ reduction, finite-precision hardware behavior or learned adaptive halting.

checks.claim: Universal cubic residual coefficient kappa(f)/6
checks.explanation: For the constant-family construction, the logistic approximation generally has a nonzero third derivative. Subtracting the two Taylor expansions therefore gives a coefficient involving $f^{\prime\prime\prime}(\theta_f)-\mathrm{TG}^{\prime\prime\prime}(\theta_f)$, rather than $f^{\prime\prime\prime}(\theta_f)$ alone. This remains a problem for smooth activations that are not themselves logistic. Separately, $C^3$ regularity supports a remainder $o(|x-\theta_f|^3)$; an $O(|x-\theta_f|^4)$ remainder needs stronger regularity.
checks.demonstration:
Write $\sigma(x)=(1+e^{-x})^{-1}$ and consider the smooth saturating activation
$$f(x)=\frac{\sigma(x)+\sigma(2x)}2.$$
Its derivative is bounded. Each summand has positive second derivative for $x<0$ and negative second derivative for $x>0$, so $f$ has its unique inflection at $\theta_f=0$. Its limits are $0$ and $1$, and both asymptotic slopes are zero. Thus it satisfies the well-behaved condition without requiring the permitted secondary tail sign changes.

Use the constant branches $c_1=1$, $c_2=0$, as in the paper's constant family. The lemma prescribes $\tau=4f'(0)=3/2$, giving $T(x)=\sigma(3x/2)$. Their values and first two derivatives agree:
$$f(0)=T(0)=\frac12,\qquad f'(0)=T'(0)=\frac38,\qquad f''(0)=T''(0)=0.$$
But
$$f^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)=-\frac9{16},\qquad T^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)=-\frac{27}{64}.$$
Hence
$$|f(x)-T(x)|=\frac3{128}|x|^3+O(x^4),$$
whereas the lemma gives $(3/32)|x|^3+O(x^4)$. The difference in cubic coefficients cannot be absorbed into an $O(x^4)$ remainder. Even the exact case $f=T=\sigma$ contradicts the universal coefficient: its residual is zero while the claimed coefficient is $1/48$.

This construction uses the lemma's explicit constant-family prescription. Theorem 8's proof instead makes both affine branches pass through $f(\theta_f)$; if both branches are constant, that instruction makes them identical and cannot produce the nontrivial constant family. The two prescriptions need to be distinguished. Reading the preceding paragraph as concentrating on approximate conversion does not resolve the coefficient error: the mixture above is not a single logistic function.
checks.repair:
State the approximation result for an explicitly chosen $T=\mathrm{TG}$ and require
$$f^{(j)}(\theta_f)=T^{(j)}(\theta_f),\qquad j=0,1,2.$$
If $f,T\in C^4$ on a neighborhood of $\theta_f$, Taylor's theorem applied to $R=f-T$ gives
$$R(\theta_f+h)=\frac{f^{\prime\prime\prime}(\theta_f)-T^{\prime\prime\prime}(\theta_f)}6h^3+O(h^4).$$
The inequality $\bigl||a+b|-|a|\bigr|\le |b|$ then gives the corrected absolute-residual formula. With only $C^3$ regularity, replace $O(h^4)$ by $o(|h|^3)$.

For the constant family, specify $T(x)=c_2+(c_1-c_2)\sigma(\tau(x-\theta_f))$ directly. Value matching requires $c_1+c_2=2f(\theta_f)$; slope matching uses the stated $\tau$, provided $c_1\ne c_2$ and the resulting $\tau>0$; second derivatives then agree at an inflection. This avoids the intersecting-branch instruction in Theorem 8. For a multiplicative construction whose branches meet at $\theta_f$, also require $f'(\theta_f)=(s_++s_-)/2$; choosing a positive $\tau$ from the second derivative does not itself enforce that equality. These conditions prove a local residual statement. They do not derive a training-stability or trainable-depth law from the corrected residual coefficient.
checks.scope: The constant-family clause of Lemma 9 has an incorrect cubic coefficient, including for a $C^\infty$ activation with a unique inflection and exact matching through second order. The correction is a conditional local Taylor formula with explicit matching and regularity assumptions. It does not establish that every well-behaved activation admits those matches, or that the residual coefficient determines training stability or trainable depth.

checks.claim: At most one inflection for all K=2 TG parameters
checks.explanation: The logistic gate has one inflection, but multiplying it by an affine branch changes the curvature. The paper's exact two-branch representation of SiLU already has two inflection points. More generally, every finite-sharpness two-branch blend with unequal slopes has exactly two. Definition 7 permits secondary tail sign changes, so the count alone does not show that SiLU violates that broader definition.
checks.demonstration:
Choose $\tau=1$, $\theta=0$, slopes $s_1=1$, $s_2=0$, and intercepts $c_1=c_2=0$. These are the paper's admitted SiLU parameters, and the activation is $T(x)=x\sigma(x)$. Differentiation gives
$$T''(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))\bigl[2+x(1-2\sigma(x))\bigr].$$
At zero, $T''(0)=1/2>0$. At both $x=4$ and $x=-4$, the bracket equals $2-4\tanh(2)<0$: indeed $e^4>1+4>3$ implies $\tanh(2)>1/2$. Continuity therefore gives a sign-changing curvature zero on each side of zero. Thus this allowed $K=2$ activation has at least two inflections.

The general calculation below shows that it has exactly two and identifies the missing parameter restriction behind the one-inflection assertion.
checks.repair:
Replace the universal one-inflection assertion with the exact classification for finite $\tau>0$. Write
$$T(x)=s_2x+c_2+(ax+b)g(x),\quad a=s_1-s_2,\quad b=c_1-c_2,\quad g(x)=\sigma(\tau(x-\theta)).$$
With $t=\tau(x-\theta)$ and $d=\tau(a\theta+b)$,
$$T''(x)=\tau g(x)(1-g(x))\bigl[2a-(at+d)\tanh(t/2)\bigr].$$
If $a\ne0$, every curvature zero has $t\ne0$ and solves
$$F(t)=t+\frac da-2\coth(t/2)=0.$$
Here $\coth u=1/\tanh u$ and $\operatorname{csch}u=1/\sinh u$. On each half-line,
$$F'(t)=1+\operatorname{csch}^2(t/2)>0.$$
The limits of $F$ are $-\infty$ and $+\infty$ at the two ends of each half-line, so each has exactly one simple root. Each root changes the curvature sign. Consequently, unequal slopes give exactly two inflections.

If $a=0$ and $b\ne0$, the activation is an affine function plus a nonzero multiple of a logistic function and has exactly one inflection, at $\theta$. If $a=b=0$, it is affine and has none. A one-inflection guarantee can therefore be retained by restricting to equal slopes. This classification describes curvature; the matching, regularity, and training assumptions in Lemma 9 and its corollaries still need to be stated separately.
checks.scope: The universal inflection-count assertion for the scalar $K=2$ blend is false. For finite $\tau>0$, equal slopes give at most one inflection and unequal slopes give exactly two. Definition 7 already permits secondary tail sign changes; two inflections alone do not contradict that definition or establish an optimization failure.
checks.title: Two affine branches can give two inflection points
checks.whyItMatters: A restriction on the number of gates is not the same as a restriction to one curvature change. The corrected classification identifies which branch parameters actually enforce a one-inflection shape.
checks.claimContext: The paragraph “Why $K=2$ suffices” states that a single logistic gate admits at most one inflection for every learned choice of gate sharpness, threshold, slopes, and intercepts. It uses this statement to argue that the architecture enforces the conditions of Lemma 9 and its corollaries. The relevant activation is the affine-branch blend, not the logistic gate alone.

checks.explanation: Differentiating the loss gradient $(f-y)f'x$ produces residual coefficient $(f-y)f''$. The printed formula reverses it. Dropping the residual removes the term under either sign, leaving the subsequent Gauss–Newton derivatives unchanged.
checks.demonstration:

$$\nabla_wL=(f(z)-y)f'(z)x,$$

$$H_{\rm GN}'(z)=2f'(z)f''(z)xx^\top,$$
$$H_{\rm GN}''(z)=2\{f''(z)^2+f'(z)f'''(z)\}xx^\top.$$
At an inflection, these give $H_{\rm GN}'=0$ and $H_{\rm GN}''=2f'f'''xx^\top$, as in the source. These identities concern the chosen approximation, not an unconditional replacement of the full Hessian.

checks.location: Corollary 11; Appendix B; PDF pages 6 and 11–12
checks.claim: In the cited random-network edge-of-chaos setting, maximum trainable depth is proportional to the inverse square of the activation’s third derivative at its inflection.
checks.explanation:
The cited theory retains both a Gaussian moment and the initialization variance. For $X_q\sim\mathcal N(0,q)$, write
$$N_f(q)=\mathbb E[f'(X_q)^2],\qquad D_f(q)=\mathbb E[f''(X_q)^2].$$
Hayou et al.’s correlation-propagation scale is $\beta_q=2N_f(q)/(qD_f(q))$. A local third derivative alone does not determine these factors. Convergence to a variance fixed point as depth increases does not make that fixed point independent of the activation or initialization.
checks.demonstration:
First keep the activation fixed: $f(x)=\tanh x$ has inflection zero and $\kappa(f)=2$. For any $q>0$, define $A_f(q)=\mathbb E[f(X_q)^2]$ and choose the initialization variances
$$\sigma_w^2=\frac1{N_f(q)},\qquad \sigma_b^2=q-\frac{A_f(q)}{N_f(q)}.$$
Strict Gaussian Poincaré gives $A_f(q)<qN_f(q)$, so the bias variance is positive. These choices satisfy the variance fixed-point equation and the edge-of-chaos condition $\sigma_w^2N_f(q)=1$. The increasing, strictly concave variance map has this point as its unique attracting fixed point.

As $q\downarrow0$, $N_f(q)\to1$ and $D_f(q)\sim4q$. Consequently,
$$\beta_q\sim\frac{1}{2q^2}\longrightarrow\infty,$$
although $\kappa(f)$ remains exactly $2$. Thus the initialization dependence cannot be discarded, even when the local curvature approximation is accurate.

A second example keeps the limiting variance at $q=1$. For $0<a\leq1/2$, take
$$f_a(x)=\int_0^x e^{-at^2-t^4}\,dt.$$
These functions are smooth, odd, bounded and increasing, with a unique inflection at zero. Their derivatives satisfy
$$f_a'(x)=e^{-ax^2-x^4},\qquad f_a''(x)=-(2ax+4x^3)e^{-ax^2-x^4},\qquad \kappa(f_a)=2a.$$
For $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, dominated convergence gives
$$N_{f_a}(1)\longrightarrow\mathbb E[e^{-2Z^4}]>0,\qquad D_{f_a}(1)\longrightarrow16\mathbb E[Z^6e^{-2Z^4}]>0.$$
The exact scale $\beta_1$ therefore has a positive finite limit, while $\kappa(f_a)^{-2}=1/(4a^2)$ diverges. Each activation admits the valid edge-of-chaos initializer above with $q=1$. This example varies initialization with the activation; it is a comparison across the corollary’s allowed settings, not a fixed-initialization experiment.

The local Taylor expansion exists in both examples. For the family $f_a$, the neighborhood in which its leading term dominates shrinks as $a\downarrow0$, while the preactivation variance stays fixed. This prevents a uniform reduction of the Gaussian curvature moment to its leading local term. The first example establishes a separate point: initialization dependence remains even when that approximation is accurate.
checks.title: The local third derivative does not determine the propagation depth scale
checks.claimContext: The paper defines $\kappa(f)=|f^{\prime\prime\prime}(\theta_f)|$ at an activation’s inflection and states an inverse-square law for maximum trainable depth. Appendix B replaces the Gaussian curvature moment by a local Taylor approximation. It qualifies that approximation by a neighborhood containing most preactivations, and separately asserts that this neighborhood covers its listed activations at practical depths.
checks.whyItMatters: The same activation can have very different propagation scales under different valid initializations. Ranking activations by $\kappa$ alone therefore omits quantities that the cited theory still depends on.
checks.scope: The unrestricted activation-only deduction in Corollary 11 and Appendix B is false. A quantified Gaussian-remainder condition supports the conditional replacement above. Hayou et al.’s scale describes correlation propagation at initialization; it is not an optimizer-independent maximum trainable depth. Conclusions about the paper’s reported training measurements or its practical Taylor neighborhoods require separate evidence.
checks.repair:
Retain the full initialization-dependent scale and state a quantitative condition for any local approximation. Let $f''(\theta)=0$, $\kappa=|f'''(\theta)|>0$, and define the remainder
$$R(X_q)=f''(X_q)-f'''(\theta)(X_q-\theta).$$
If its Gaussian $L^2$ norm satisfies $\|R\|_2\leq\rho\kappa\sqrt{q+\theta^2}$ for $0\leq\rho<1$, the triangle and reverse-triangle inequalities give
$$\frac{2N_f(q)}{q(1+\rho)^2\kappa^2(q+\theta^2)}\leq\beta_q\leq\frac{2N_f(q)}{q(1-\rho)^2\kappa^2(q+\theta^2)}.$$
This is a sufficient conditional replacement. A local derivative bound must also control the Gaussian-weighted remainder outside its neighborhood. A uniform inverse-square comparison additionally needs upper and lower bounds on $N_f(q)/[q(q+\theta^2)]$ and a uniform error parameter below one. An asymptotic proportionality requires a specified limit and convergence of the remaining factors.

checks.claim: Any continuous function admits an error-epsilon piecewise-linear interpolant with K=O(1/epsilon) pieces, and sigmoid-gated TG inherits this guarantee.
checks.explanation: A continuous function can contain increasingly many oscillations at successively smaller scales. Continuity ensures that approximation error tends to zero as the mesh shrinks, but it does not impose the claimed rate. A finite-temperature sigmoid gate also approximates a hard piecewise-linear interpolant rather than equaling it.
checks.whyItMatters: A branch budget needs a quantitative regularity assumption. Continuity alone can require faster growth than the proposed inverse-error rate.
checks.claimContext: Section 2.4 motivates the branch count by claiming that every continuous function has a piecewise-linear approximation with $K=O(1/\varepsilon)$ pieces at error $\varepsilon$. It then transfers that rate to sigmoid-gated Threshold Gating (TG). Here $K$ is the number of affine pieces. No domain or regularity bound accompanies the claim; even on $[0,1]$, continuity alone is insufficient.
checks.scope: The defect concerns the universal piece-count rate and its transfer to finite-temperature TG. The corrected guarantee requires a compact domain and explicit target regularity, with a separate smoothing error. It does not refute approximation with unrestricted branch count and sharpness, establish efficient training, or prove universality with a fixed two-branch model.
checks.demonstration:
For each integer $n\geq1$, put a triangular tent on $I_n=[2^{-n},2^{1-n}]$, with value zero at both endpoints and height $n^{-1/2}$ at its midpoint. Set $f(0)=0$. These tents define one continuous function on $[0,1]$, since their heights tend to zero. Let $p$ be a piecewise-affine function with $K$ pieces and $\|f-p\|_\infty\leq\varepsilon_n=1/(4\sqrt n)$. Each of the first $n$ tents has height at least $4\varepsilon_n$. If $p$ had no breakpoint inside one of those intervals, its midpoint value would be the average of its endpoint values, hence at most $\varepsilon_n$. Approximating the peak requires at least $3\varepsilon_n$, a contradiction. Thus each interval needs an interior breakpoint and
$$K\geq n+1,\qquad \varepsilon_n K\geq\frac{n+1}{4\sqrt n}\longrightarrow\infty.$$
No constant in $K=O(1/\varepsilon)$ works for this fixed continuous target.
checks.repair:
State a compact interval $[a,b]$ and the target’s modulus of continuity $\omega_f(h)=\sup_{|x-y|\leq h}|f(x)-f(y)|$. Linear interpolation on a mesh of width at most $h$ has uniform error at most $\omega_f(h)$. If $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz and $D=b-a$, the sharper bound $Lh/2$ gives $K=O(LD/\varepsilon)$ pieces as $\varepsilon\to0$.

Account for sigmoid smoothing separately. Write the interpolant as an affine term plus hinges $\sum_j d_j(x-t_j)_+$, where $u_+=\max\{u,0\}$ and $d_j$ is the slope change at knot $t_j$. Replace each hinge by $(x-t_j)\sigma(\tau(x-t_j))$, with $\sigma(z)=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}$ and finite sharpness $\tau>0$. Since
$$|u\sigma(\tau u)-u_+|=\frac{|u|}{1+e^{\tau|u|}}\leq\frac1{e\tau},$$
the additional uniform error is at most $\sum_j|d_j|/(e\tau)$. Ordered cumulative logistic gates express this smoothed hinge sum in TG form. Choose the mesh and sharpness so that interpolation and smoothing each contribute at most $\varepsilon/2$. This proves the stated regularity-dependent approximation guarantee for finite-temperature gates.

checks.claim: For f(x)=x h(x) with a well-behaved factor h, the zero second derivative of the identity factor reduces the product bound to at most two inflections and three branches.
checks.explanation: The relevant curvature is $F^{\prime\prime}(x)=2h^{\prime}(x)+xh^{\prime\prime}(x)$. checks.claimContext: Remarks 12–13 infer an inflection bound from the component functions, then use it to motivate at most three TG branches. Remark 13 applies this reasoning to $F(x)=xh(x)$: because the identity factor has zero second derivative and $h$ is well-behaved, it asserts at most two inflections. Here $m$ counts inflections and $K$ counts branches.
checks.scope: The counterexample refutes the general identity-product inference under a strict one-inflection premise. The two-inflection counts for GELU, SiLU and Mish remain valid by their separate derivative calculations. It does not establish or disprove exact three-branch representations, and it concerns the product rule rather than the inflection classification of a two-branch TG blend.
checks.demonstration:
Choose an even smooth cutoff $\chi$ with $0\leq\chi\leq1$, supported where $0.9<|x|<2.1$ and equal to one on $1\leq|x|\leq2$. Define
$$q(x)=(1-\chi(x))2x+\chi(x)\frac2x\left[1+\frac14\sin(10\pi|x|)\right],\qquad h^{\prime}(x)=\exp\left(-\int_0^xq(t)\,dt\right),\qquad h(0)=0.$$
The cutoff makes the apparent singularity at zero removable. The function $q$ is odd and has the sign of $x$. Hence $h^{\prime}>0$ and $h^{\prime\prime}=-qh^{\prime}$ changes sign exactly once, at zero. Outside a compact set, $h^{\prime}$ is a constant multiple of $e^{-x^2}$, so $h$ is smooth, bounded and increasing with bounded derivative. For $F(x)=xh(x)$, the derivative $F^{\prime}=h+xh^{\prime}$ is bounded and its asymptotic slopes are finite. Nevertheless, on $1\leq x\leq2$,
$$F^{\prime\prime}(x)=-\frac12h^{\prime}(x)\sin(10\pi x).$$
This has nine strict sign changes at $x=k/10$ for $k=11,\ldots,19$; even symmetry gives nine more at negative inputs. Thus the general product rule fails even with a strictly one-inflection factor and no secondary tail inflections.
checks.repair:
Replace the general component-count argument with derivative sign calculations for the named activations. For GELU,
$$f^{\prime\prime}(x)=(2-x^2)\varphi(x),$$
where $\varphi$ is the standard normal density, giving exactly two inflections at $\pm\sqrt2$. For SiLU,
$$f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\sigma^{\prime}(x)[2-x\tanh(x/2)],$$
where $\sigma$ is the logistic function. Since $x\tanh(x/2)$ increases strictly with $|x|$, there is exactly one root on each side of zero.

Mish also has exactly two inflections. Write $f(x)=xH(x)$ with $H(x)=\tanh(\log(1+e^x))$, and set $r=e^x$. Then
$$\frac{H^{\prime\prime}(x)}{H^{\prime}(x)}=g(r)=1+\frac r{r+1}-\frac{4r(r+1)}{r^2+2r+2}.$$
The function $g$ decreases strictly from $1$ to $-2$, with $g(1)=-1/10$. Thus $2+xg(e^x)$ has one zero in each tail and none in the intervening region where $xg(e^x)\geq0$. These calculations justify the named two-inflection counts. Turning an inflection count into a branch-count guarantee still requires a separate representation or approximation argument.

checks.demonstration:
Take the shifted quadratic $f(x)=(x-1)^2/2$. It is globally $L$-smooth and $\mu$-strongly convex with $L=\mu=1$, and its minimizer is $x^*=1$. Use exact gradients, so the permitted oracle parameters are $\zeta=\alpha=0$. Initialize $x_0=y_0=x_1=1$. This also agrees with the original three-sequence method at $k=0$, so the example does not rely on the printed omission of an initialization for $x_1$.

Write $\Gamma_k=\sum_{i=0}^k\gamma_i$, with $\gamma_0=\Gamma_0=1$, and use the positive-root schedule
$$2L+\frac\mu2\Gamma_k=\frac{2L\gamma_{k+1}^2}{\Gamma_{k+1}}.$$
It gives $\gamma_1\approx1.90587$ and $\gamma_2\approx3.26366$. At the first printed recurrence step, $y_1=1$ and the exact gradient is zero, yet substitution yields
$$x_2=1-\frac{\Gamma_0}{\Gamma_1}+\frac{\gamma_1}{4\gamma_2}\approx0.80186.$$
The gradient step producing the theorem's target iterate is $y_2=x_2-f'(x_2)/(2L)=(x_2+1)/2$, so
$$y_2\approx0.90093,\qquad f(y_2)-f^*\approx0.00490741>0.$$
Theorem 3.3 gives zero on its right-hand side, since the initial radius $R$ and oracle error $\zeta$ are both zero. The printed update therefore violates the claimed bound at $y_2$, not only at an auxiliary iterate. Exact elimination of the third sequence gives a different coefficient of $y_k$ and keeps this initialized minimizer fixed; the failure concerns the printed recurrence, not accelerated convergence with inexact gradients in general.
checks.repair:
Let $\Gamma_k=\sum_{i=0}^k\gamma_i$, $r_k=\gamma_k/\gamma_{k+1}$, $s_k=\Gamma_{k-1}/\Gamma_k$ and $\tau_k=\gamma_{k+1}/\Gamma_{k+1}$. Eliminating the third sequence from the original method gives the corrected recurrence
$$x_{k+1}=(1-\tau_k+r_k)y_k-r_ks_ky_{k-1}+r_k\frac{\mu}{4L}x_k.$$
Use the original three-sequence initialization at $k=0$. This restores exact equivalence with that method, including preservation of a constant sequence at the minimizer. With oracle parameters
$$(\tilde L,\tilde\mu,\delta)=\left(2L,\mu/2,\left(\frac1{2L}+\frac1\mu\right)\zeta^2\right),$$
Theorem 7 of Devolder–Glineur–Nesterov gives
$$f(y_k)-f^*\le\min\left\{\frac{8LR}{k^2},2LR\exp\left(-\frac k4\sqrt{\frac\mu L}\right)\right\}+\left(1+2\sqrt{\frac L\mu}\right)\left(\frac1{2L}+\frac1\mu\right)\zeta^2.$$

Let \(G=(M,1)\), \(c=(1,4)\), \(R=1\), with \(M>2\). Greedy buys the first item because \(c_1<c_2\), immediately meeting coverage at cost \(M\). The second item alone meets coverage at cost two and is optimal:

\[\frac{\omega(S_{\mathrm{greedy}})}{\omega(S^*)}=\frac M2\longrightarrow\infty.\]

This is a legal paper-derived requirement: with \(n=2\), \(D=1\), \(\Gamma=M/2\), the formula \(R=\sum_iG_i-n\Gamma/D\) gives one. Choose \(\epsilon>\Gamma\). Convex losses \(f_1(x)=Mx\), \(f_2(x)=x\) on \([0,1]\) realize the Lipschitz bounds. At \(M=100\), the ratio is fifty.
checks.repair:
Enumerate an item-cost threshold \(W\). Discard items with \(\omega_i>W\), solve the remaining fractional covering problem in decreasing \(v_i/\omega_i\) order, and round the last fractional item up. Keep the cheapest feasible candidate over all thresholds. Zero-cost items may first be included freely.

Let \(W\) be the largest item cost in an optimal integral solution. That solution remains available, so the fractional optimum costs at most \(\mathrm{OPT}\). At most one item is rounded, adding at most \(W\le\mathrm{OPT}\). Therefore

\[\omega(S_{\mathrm{repaired}})\le\mathrm{OPT}+W\le2\mathrm{OPT}.\]

This modest modification proves a factor-two guarantee for the displayed knapsack objective.
checks.scope: The guarantee concerns the sum \(\sum_{i\in S}G_i\sqrt{c_i}\). Squaring that sum gives at most a factor-four guarantee for the conservative numerator.
